items.title: Push CO2 hard enough and it becomes neither gas nor liquid
items.claim: Above 31.1°C and 73.8 bar, carbon dioxide enters a 'supercritical' state — it fills its container like a gas but has the density and solvent power of a liquid. It is now the standard solvent for decaffeinating coffee.
items.prompt: Why is supercritical CO2 useful for extracting compounds from natural materials?

options.text: It penetrates porous solids like a gas, dissolves organics like a liquid, and can be removed cleanly by depressurisation — leaving no solvent residue
It is the only solvent that dissolves caffeine

items.reveal:
On a pressure-temperature phase diagram, the liquid-gas boundary terminates at a critical point. Beyond it, the distinction between liquid and gas disappears — there is a single fluid phase whose density can be tuned continuously by changing pressure.

For CO2 the critical point is at 31.1°C and 73.8 bar — easily reachable in industrial equipment. Supercritical CO2 dissolves caffeine but not the flavour compounds in coffee beans. After extraction, depressurising vaporises the CO2 instantly with no residue.

Applications: hop extraction for beer, essential oil isolation, dry cleaning, semiconductor cleaning, dyeing textiles without water, and recently as a working fluid in highly efficient power-cycle generators.
items.why: Phase diagrams in GCSE end at the liquid-gas boundary. The fluid beyond the critical point has properties of both — and quietly underpins major industries.

items.title: Water dissolves more things than any other liquid
items.claim: Water is called 'the universal solvent'. It dissolves more substances than any other liquid — salts, sugars, gases, many organic molecules. Yet it has only three atoms and a simple structure.
items.prompt: What makes water such a versatile solvent?

options.text: Water is highly polar (large dipole), forms hydrogen bonds with H-bond donors and acceptors, and has a high dielectric constant (around 80) that weakens ionic attractions enough for ions to separate and become solvated
Water is the only liquid on Earth that occurs naturally

items.reveal:
Water's bent shape and large O-H bond polarity give a permanent dipole moment of 1.85 debye. Each water molecule can form up to 4 hydrogen bonds — two as donor, two as acceptor.

Water's dielectric constant of about 80 (vs about 2 for hexane) means it screens ionic charges strongly: a cation and anion that would attract each other electrostatically in vacuum are 80 times less attracted in water, so they separate.

Non-polar substances (oils, wax) lack matching interactions and so won't dissolve. 'Universal' is overstating things — water is just a brilliant solvent for polar and ionic species, and we mostly care about polar and ionic species.
items.why: Water is treated as a passive background. Its chemistry actively shapes whether ions stay dissolved or precipitate.

items.title: Hafnium and zirconium are almost impossible to tell apart
items.claim: Zirconium and hafnium sit one above the other in Group 4 — separated by the entire lanthanide row. They have almost identical atomic radii (160 vs 159 pm), nearly identical ionic radii, and remarkably similar chemistry.
items.prompt: Why doesn't hafnium have a larger radius like the down-group trend predicts?

options.text: Hafnium has fewer electrons than expected

The 14 lanthanide elements between them add 14 protons but the 4f electrons screen the nucleus very poorly, so the effective nuclear charge experienced by the 5d and 6s shells in Hf is much higher than down-group trends suggest — the 'lanthanide contraction'
Hafnium atoms are crushed by gravity

items.reveal:
Across the 14 lanthanides, atomic number rises by 14 but the added electrons go into 4f orbitals 'inside' the 6s shell. Because 4f electrons screen poorly, the outer electrons see steadily more effective nuclear charge — and the atomic radius shrinks across the row.

By the time you reach hafnium (Z=72), the radius is essentially the same as zirconium (Z=40, four periods up the table). The two elements are chemically near-identical and have to be separated by very fine techniques — typically ion exchange chromatography.

Nuclear reactor design depends on the separation. Zirconium is used for fuel-rod cladding (very low neutron absorption); hafnium has a neutron cross-section about 600 times higher and is used for control rods. Mixing them up is catastrophic.
items.why: Down-group similarity is taught; lateral similarity caused by f-shell shielding is a hidden consequence of the full periodic table.
